fields.Prompt: King of Qin who conquered the other six states and in 221 BCE declared himself first emperor of a unified China.
fields.Extra: Born Ying Zheng. The title huangdi he coined borrowed from the legendary sovereigns and emperors.

fields.Prompt: Qin chancellor who standardized the script, drove the Legalist program, and was executed by Zhao Gao.
fields.Extra: A student of Xunzi. He said he took his idea of merit from watching rats: those in the granary fed better than those in the latrine.

fields.Prompt: Some 8,000 individually modelled figures buried in pits near Qin Shi Huang's tomb, found by well-diggers in 1974.
fields.Extra: Once brightly painted: the pigment flakes away within minutes of meeting the air, one reason excavation goes slowly.

fields.Prompt: Qin Shi Huang's unexcavated tomb mound near Xi'an, described as containing rivers of this liquid.
fields.Extra: Soil surveys really do show anomalous mercury concentrations, which is one reason the mound is still unopened.

fields.Prompt: Substance Qin Shi Huang consumed in pursuit of immortality, which probably killed him.
fields.Extra: His alchemists prescribed it as an elixir. He died in 210 BCE on tour in the east.

fields.Prompt: Qin general who drove back the Xiongnu and linked existing walls into an early version of the Great Wall.
fields.Extra: Forced to take his own life in the succession purge after 210 BCE.

fields.Prompt: Qin policy, reported by Sima Qian, of destroying philosophical texts and executing scholars.
fields.Answer: the burning of books and burying of scholars
fields.Extra: Treat with care: the account grew in the telling, the “burying” may have been one purge of alchemists, and the fullest version postdates the Qin by centuries.

fields.Prompt: Eunuch who concealed Qin Shi Huang's death in a cart of rotting fish, forged the succession, and destroyed Li Si.
fields.Extra: He tested his officials' loyalty by presenting a deer and calling it a horse — still an idiom for enforced absurdity.

fields.Prompt: Puppet second emperor installed by Zhao Gao in place of the designated heir Fusu.
fields.Extra: Huhai, Qin Shi Huang's own son. The dynasty outlived its founder by four years.

fields.Prompt: 209 BCE uprising of conscripts under Chen Sheng and Wu Guang, the first revolt against the Qin.
fields.Extra: They were late to a post on pain of death, so rebelled instead — and planted a silk message in a fish to fake a prophecy.

fields.Prompt: Peasant-born rebel who defeated Xiang Yu and founded the Han dynasty.
fields.Extra: Reigned as Emperor Gaozu. The first commoner to found a Chinese dynasty.

fields.Prompt: Chu aristocrat and warlord who destroyed the Qin army at Julu but lost the subsequent civil war to Liu Bang.
fields.Extra: When he threatened to boil Liu Bang's captured father, Liu Bang asked to be sent a cup of the soup.

fields.Prompt: Banquet at which Xiang Yu's followers tried and failed to assassinate Liu Bang.
fields.Extra: The Swan Goose Gate feast. A byword for a meal that is really an ambush.

fields.Prompt: 202 BCE battle that ended the Chu–Han contention and left Liu Bang master of China.
fields.Extra: Xiang Yu, surrounded, heard Chu songs from the enemy camp, and concluded his homeland had fallen — hence the idiom for hopeless encirclement.

fields.Prompt: Dynasty of 206 BCE to 220 CE that gave the Chinese ethnic majority its name.
fields.Extra: Split by Wang Mang's usurpation into Western (capital Chang'an) and Eastern (capital Luoyang).

fields.Prompt: First empress of the Han, who had her rival Lady Qi mutilated and displayed as a “human swine.”
fields.Extra: Lü Zhi. Her son was said never to have recovered from being shown it.

fields.Prompt: Han emperor of a 54-year reign who made Confucianism the state doctrine and shattered the Xiongnu.
fields.Extra: Wu Di. No later emperor reigned as long until the Kangxi Emperor.

fields.Prompt: Nomadic confederation north of the Han, bought off with princesses and tribute before Emperor Wu went on the offensive.
fields.Extra: The appeasement policy was heqin, “peace marriage.”

fields.Prompt: Envoy sent west by Emperor Wu to find allies against the Xiongnu, whose reports opened the Silk Road.
fields.Extra: He was held captive by the Xiongnu for years, married there, and still completed the mission.

fields.Prompt: Historian who wrote the Shiji, and chose castration over suicide so as to finish it.
fields.Extra: He was punished for defending the general Li Ling. The father of Chinese historiography.

fields.Prompt: Sima Qian's history, covering from the Yellow Emperor to his own day and organizing material by annals, treatises, and biographies.
fields.Extra: The Shiji. Its structure set the pattern for every later dynastic history.

fields.Prompt: Court debate of 81 BCE over state monopolies on two commodities, recorded in a famous text.
fields.Extra: Confucian reformers argued the monopolies corrupted government; the officials answered that they paid for the frontier. Huan Kuan wrote it up a generation later.

fields.Prompt: Regent who usurped the Han throne in 9 CE and founded the short-lived Xin dynasty.
fields.Extra: His land nationalization and currency reforms failed spectacularly; he was killed in 23 CE.

fields.Prompt: Peasant rebellion that helped destroy Wang Mang, whose fighters painted their faces to tell friend from foe.
fields.Extra: They set up a puppet Han heir, proved an ungovernable mob, and surrendered to Liu Xiu — the future Emperor Guangwu.

fields.Prompt: Emperor who restored the Han in 25 CE and moved the capital to Luoyang.
fields.Extra: Liu Xiu.

fields.Prompt: Eunuch credited in 105 CE with the process for making paper from bark, hemp, and rags.
fields.Extra: Paper existed before him; his contribution was a process cheap enough to displace bamboo strips and silk.

fields.Prompt: Han polymath who built the first seismoscope, a bronze vessel that dropped a ball from a dragon's mouth toward a distant earthquake.
fields.Extra: He also argued that the moon shines by reflected sunlight.

fields.Prompt: General who pushed Han power to the Caspian and secured the Silk Road's western reaches.
fields.Extra: His brother Ban Gu wrote the Book of Han.

fields.Prompt: First known woman historian of China, who finished her brother's Book of Han and wrote Lessons for Women.
fields.Extra: Lessons for Women counsels humility and obedience; she also tutored the young Empress Deng.

fields.Prompt: 184 CE Daoist-inspired peasant rising led by Zhang Jue, whose followers wore a coloured headscarf.
fields.Extra: Its suppression put armies in the hands of regional commanders, which is how the Han actually ended.

fields.Prompt: Daoist movement founded by Zhang Daoling, named for the contribution required to join.
fields.Answer: the Way of the Five Pecks of Rice
fields.Extra: He is counted the first Celestial Master.

fields.Prompt: Warlord who seized Luoyang, deposed one boy emperor for another, and burned the capital when driven out.
fields.Extra: Killed by his bodyguard and adopted son, Lü Bu. Melting bronze statues down for coin wrecked the currency.

fields.Prompt: Clique of palace eunuchs, twelve of them despite the group's name, who dominated the court of Emperor Ling.
fields.Extra: Their grip on Emperor Ling provoked the purge that let Dong Zhuo march into Luoyang — the beginning of the end for the Han.

fields.Prompt: The three states that divided China from 220 to 280.
fields.Extra: Cao Wei in the north, Shu Han in Sichuan, Eastern Wu on the lower Yangtze.

fields.Prompt: 208 battle on the Yangtze at which a fire attack and a shift of wind destroyed Cao Cao's fleet.
fields.Extra: Chibi. The allied victory of Liu Bei and Sun Quan fixed the three-way split.

fields.Prompt: Warlord who took the Han emperor under his protection and ruled the north in his name.
fields.Extra: Also a serious poet and a commentator on The Art of War. His son Cao Pi took the throne as the first Wei emperor.

fields.Prompt: 200 CE battle at which Cao Cao, heavily outnumbered, destroyed Yuan Shao and won northern China.
fields.Extra: Cao Cao won it by burning Yuan Shao's supply depot at Wuchao: the textbook logistics strike.

fields.Prompt: Ruler of Shu Han, a distant Han relative who built a following on claims of virtue and legitimacy.
fields.Extra: His capital was Chengdu.

fields.Prompt: Shu chancellor nicknamed the Crouching Dragon, who devised the Longzhong Plan.
fields.Extra: His northern expeditions all failed. The novel turned him into a near-magician.

fields.Prompt: Shu general deified as a god of war and worshipped for loyalty, executed after losing Jing Province.
fields.Extra: Deified as Guandi and worshipped for loyalty ever since, by police and criminal societies alike.

fields.Prompt: Founder of Eastern Wu, whose capital Jianye is modern Nanjing.
fields.Extra: The longest-lived of the three founders; he outlasted both Cao Cao and Liu Bei and declared himself emperor last.

fields.Prompt: 222 battle at which Lu Xun's Wu forces burned Liu Bei's camps, ending Shu's attempt to avenge Guan Yu.
fields.Extra: Also Xiaoting.

fields.Prompt: Wei general who feigned illness and senility, then seized the state in the 249 coup at the Gaoping Tombs.
fields.Extra: His grandson Sima Yan turned the Sima grip into the Jin dynasty.

fields.Prompt: Ming novel that made the period a national epic, opening on the observation that what is long divided must unite.
fields.Extra: By Luo Guanzhong, written over a thousand years after the events — and clued more often than the history it dramatizes.

fields.Prompt: Dynasty founded in 266 when Sima Yan deposed the last Wei emperor, which briefly reunified China in 280.
fields.Extra: The Sima clan's Jin (晉) — not the later Jurchen Jin (金) of the 12th century.

fields.Prompt: Civil war among Sima princes that wrecked the Western Jin within a generation.
fields.Answer: the War of the Eight Princes
fields.Extra: Sixteen years of Sima princes destroying one another, which is what let the northern peoples into China.

fields.Prompt: 311 sack of Luoyang by Xiongnu forces, which drove the Jin court south.
fields.Extra: Emperor Huai was captured and made to pour wine for his captors at a banquet before being killed.

fields.Prompt: Non-Chinese peoples — Xiongnu, Xianbei, Jie, Di, and Qiang — who overran the north in the fourth century.
fields.Extra: Wu Hu.

fields.Prompt: Southern successor state founded at Jiankang in 317 after the north was lost.
fields.Extra: Jiankang is modern Nanjing.

fields.Prompt: 383 battle at which the vastly larger army of the Former Qin was routed, saving the Eastern Jin.
fields.Extra: The Jin statesman Xie An is said to have finished his game of Go before mentioning the victory.

fields.Prompt: Xianbei dynasty that reunified northern China in 439 and ruled it until 534.
fields.Extra: The Tuoba clan.

fields.Prompt: Northern Wei emperor who forced sinicization — Chinese dress, language, and surnames — and moved the capital to Luoyang.
fields.Extra: He changed the ruling clan's name from Tuoba to Yuan. He also introduced the equal-field system the Sui and Tang inherited.

fields.Prompt: Buddhist cave complex near Datong, carved under the Northern Wei before the capital moved.
fields.Extra: Its successor after the move is Longmen, near Luoyang.

fields.Prompt: Folk heroine of a Northern Wei ballad who takes her father's place in the army against the Rouran.
fields.Extra: The Ballad of Mulan is a few hundred words long.

fields.Prompt: Mathematician who fixed π between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927 and gave the approximation 355/113.
fields.Extra: The fraction is the Milü; nobody bettered his bounds for about nine hundred years.

fields.Prompt: The four southern dynasties ruling in turn from Jiankang between 420 and 589.
fields.Extra: The first is the Liu Song, named for its founder Liu Yu, to distinguish it from the later Song.

fields.Prompt: Liang emperor and fanatical Buddhist patron who repeatedly gave himself to a monastery and had to be ransomed back.
fields.Extra: He starved to death under house arrest after a rebellion.

fields.Prompt: Northern Zhou official who seized power in 581 and reunified China in 589, founding the Sui.
fields.Extra: Reigned as Emperor Wen of Sui.

fields.Prompt: Dynasty of 581–618 that reunified China and exhausted itself building the infrastructure the Tang inherited.
fields.Extra: Two emperors in thirty-seven years: one reunified China, the other broke it. The Tang inherited everything they built.

fields.Prompt: Sui mega-project linking the Yellow and Yangtze systems, built with conscript labour on a ruinous scale.
fields.Extra: The longest artificial waterway in the world. It made it possible to feed northern capitals on southern rice.

fields.Prompt: Sui institution of recruiting officials by written examination, which the Tang developed into a real route into office.
fields.Extra: Keju.

fields.Prompt: Sui central government structure of three policy departments over six executive ministries.
fields.Answer: the Three Departments and Six Ministries
fields.Extra: Inherited by the Tang and copied by Korea and Japan.

fields.Prompt: Profligate second Sui emperor whose invasions of Korea broke the dynasty.
fields.Extra: Sui Yang Di. Assassinated by Yuwen Huaji in 618.

fields.Prompt: 612 battle at which the Goguryeo general Ŭlchi Mundŏk destroyed a Sui army by releasing a dammed river.
fields.Extra: Of a reported 300,000 men in that column, a few thousand got back. Three invasions of Goguryeo failed and the revolts they provoked ended the Sui.

fields.Prompt: Battle at which Tang of Shang overthrew the last Xia king, founding the Shang.
fields.Extra: The defeated King Jie was exiled rather than killed — the template for a dynasty claiming it took power reluctantly.

fields.Prompt: The five works that formed the core Confucian canon and the basis of the imperial examinations.
fields.Extra: The Poetry, Documents, Rites, Changes, and Spring and Autumn Annals. A sixth, on music, is said to have been lost.

fields.Prompt: Confucian classic of divination built on sixty-four hexagrams.
fields.Extra: The Book of Changes. Consulted by casting yarrow stalks or coins.

fields.Prompt: Confucius' grandson, traditionally credited with the Doctrine of the Mean and with transmitting the teaching to Mencius' school.
fields.Extra: Kong Ji. The line Confucius to Zisi to Mencius is the orthodox transmission of the Way.

fields.Prompt: Logician of the School of Names who argued that a white horse is not a horse.
fields.Extra: The paradox turns on whether “horse” picks out a shape and “white horse” a shape plus a colour.

fields.Prompt: Sisters who led a rebellion that drove Han forces out of northern Vietnam in 40 CE.
fields.Extra: Trưng Trắc and Trưng Nhị. National heroines in Vietnam; temples to them still stand.

fields.Prompt: Han general who crushed the Trung sisters' revolt and reimposed Chinese rule on the Red River delta.
fields.Extra: He is said to have set bronze pillars to mark the empire's southern limit.

fields.Prompt: Han diplomat sent toward Rome in 97 CE who turned back at the Persian Gulf, talked out of the crossing by Parthian sailors.
fields.Extra: The Parthians had every reason to keep Han and Rome from dealing directly.

fields.Prompt: Han emperor whose infatuation with Dong Xian gave Chinese the phrase “the passion of the cut sleeve.”
fields.Extra: He reportedly cut his sleeve off rather than wake the sleeping Dong Xian.

fields.Prompt: The four texts Zhu Xi selected as the Confucian core curriculum, displacing the older Five Classics in the examinations.
fields.Extra: Analects, Mencius, Great Learning, Doctrine of the Mean. His edition governed the exams from 1313 to 1905.

fields.Prompt: Confucius' negative formulation of the golden rule.
fields.Extra: “Do not impose on others what you do not wish for yourself.” Stated as a prohibition rather than a prescription.

fields.Prompt: The five hierarchical bonds that order Confucian society.
fields.Extra: Ruler–subject, father–son, husband–wife, elder–younger brother, friend–friend. Only the last is between equals.

fields.Prompt: Confucius' remark on hearing his stable had burned, taken as proof of his priorities.
fields.Answer: he asked whether anyone was hurt
fields.Extra: He did not ask about the horses — pointed, since horses were worth more than the stablemen.

fields.Prompt: Confucius' image for government by virtue: the ruler who governs this way is like this fixed point.
fields.Extra: The other stars turn toward it without being pushed.

fields.Prompt: Song philosopher who assembled the Four Books and refounded Confucianism on a metaphysics of principle and vital force.
fields.Extra: Neo-Confucianism. His commentaries were the orthodoxy examined on for six centuries.

fields.Prompt: Honorific for Mencius as the tradition's second founder.
fields.Extra: Confucius being the first. The pairing is what makes Confucianism a school rather than one man's sayings.

fields.Prompt: Mencius' four innate moral sprouts, beginning with the feeling of compassion.
fields.Extra: Compassion, shame, deference, and the sense of right and wrong — growing into ren, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom.

fields.Prompt: The six disciplines of the classical gentleman's education.
fields.Extra: Rites, music, archery, charioteering, calligraphy, and mathematics.

fields.Prompt: Jesuit who latinized Kong Fuzi into “Confucius” and argued Chinese rites were civil rather than idolatrous.
fields.Extra: The dispute over that claim became the Chinese Rites controversy.

fields.Prompt: Assassin sent by Crown Prince Dan of Yan, who hid a dagger in a rolled map to get close to the king of Qin.
fields.Extra: He missed; the king ran round a pillar because courtiers were forbidden weapons. Yan's king later sent Dan's head to Qin in apology.

fields.Prompt: Blinded musician who hid lead in his zither and swung it at Qin Shi Huang, avenging his friend Jing Ke.
fields.Extra: He had played the zhu as Jing Ke departed on his mission to assassinate the King of Qin.

fields.Prompt: Merchant who financed the rise of Qin Shi Huang's father and served as his chancellor.
fields.Extra: Rumour made him the emperor's real father. He compiled an encyclopedia and was driven to suicide.

fields.Prompt: Lover of the queen dowager, smuggled into the palace disguised as a eunuch, whose revolt ended with him torn apart by chariots.
fields.Extra: His two sons by her were killed and the queen placed under house arrest.

fields.Prompt: Twelve giant bronze statues Qin Shi Huang cast from the confiscated weapons of the conquered states.
fields.Extra: Disarming the empire and advertising it in one act. All are lost.

fields.Prompt: Defensive work Qin Shi Huang had Meng Tian build by joining and extending the walls of the old states.
fields.Extra: Very little Qin work survives; what tourists visit is overwhelmingly Ming.

fields.Prompt: Dynasty Wang Mang proclaimed in 9 CE, meaning “new,” which lasted only as long as he did.
fields.Extra: Ended in 23 CE when rebels killed him in the Weiyang Palace.

fields.Prompt: Trade network opened by Zhang Qian's embassies, carrying silk west and Buddhism east.
fields.Extra: The name is a 19th-century coinage by Ferdinand von Richthofen, not an ancient one.

fields.Prompt: Han policy of marrying princesses to Xiongnu leaders and paying them off, abandoned by Emperor Wu.
fields.Extra: Adopted after Emperor Gaozu was trapped at Baideng in 200 BCE.

fields.Prompt: 154 BCE revolt of seven Han kingdoms against the throne's efforts to cut their power.
fields.Answer: the Rebellion of the Seven States
fields.Extra: Its defeat under Emperor Jing cleared the way for his son Emperor Wu's centralization.

fields.Prompt: Witch-hunt of 91 BCE in which Emperor Wu's heir was driven into revolt and death over accusations of sorcery.
fields.Extra: Tens of thousands died. Emperor Wu later admitted the charges were false.

fields.Prompt: Han official who ran the salt and iron monopolies and the price-stabilizing grain system.
fields.Extra: A former merchant, which his Confucian opponents never let him forget.

fields.Prompt: Imperial university founded at Chang'an to train officials in the Confucian classics.
fields.Extra: By the Eastern Han it held tens of thousands of students, and they rioted.

fields.Prompt: Empress dowager who put a hundred-day-old baby on the throne as Emperor Shang.
fields.Extra: Installing infants kept power with the consort clans, and became the Eastern Han's fatal habit.

fields.Prompt: Han emperor under whom the Yellow Turbans rose and the eunuchs ruled.
fields.Extra: He sold offices for cash and had a mock market built in the palace grounds so he could play at being a merchant.

fields.Prompt: Nomadic people who replaced the Xiongnu as the steppe threat to the later Han.
fields.Extra: Proto-Mongolic. Their descendants founded the Northern Wei and, through it, shaped the Sui and Tang ruling houses.

fields.Prompt: Visitors recorded as reaching the Han court in 166 CE from “Da Qin,” sent, they said, by a ruler called Andun.
fields.Extra: Da Qin is Rome and Andun is Marcus Aurelius Antoninus; the party were probably merchants improving their credentials.

fields.Prompt: Elite Han palace guard led at the end by the warlord Dong Zhuo.
fields.Answer: the Guards of the Feathered Forest
fields.Extra: Yulin. The Tang revived the name for the palace army the eunuchs later controlled.

fields.Prompt: Extinct elephant hunted by the first people to reach Japan across Pleistocene land bridges.
fields.Extra: Alongside the giant elk Sinomegaceros. People arrived perhaps 35,000 years ago.

fields.Prompt: Archaeologist nicknamed “God's Hands,” caught on camera in 2000 planting the “Palaeolithic” artifacts he had been discovering.
fields.Extra: His finds had pushed Japan's human history back hundreds of thousands of years; nearly all of it had to be struck from the textbooks.

fields.Prompt: Japanese prehistoric period, roughly 13,000 to 1000 BCE, named for the patterns on its pottery.
fields.Extra: Jōmon means “cord-marked.” Its pottery is among the oldest in the world.

fields.Prompt: American zoologist whose 1877 dig at the Ōmori shell mound gave Jōmon pottery its name.
fields.Extra: He described the ware as “cord marked,” and the Japanese translation stuck.

fields.Prompt: Large Jōmon settlement in Aomori Prefecture, one of Japan's earliest permanent villages.
fields.Extra: Occupied for well over a millennium and abandoned around 2300 BCE.

fields.Prompt: Jōmon clay figurines with huge goggle-like eyes.
fields.Extra: The best known is the Kamen no Megami, the “Masked Goddess.”

fields.Prompt: Comma-shaped beads found in Jōmon graves, later one of the three imperial regalia.
fields.Extra: They may have marked status.

fields.Prompt: Indigenous people of Hokkaido, Sakhalin, and the Kuril Islands.
fields.Extra: Recognized as indigenous by a Diet resolution in 2008 and in law only in 2019; the Ryukyuans are still not.

fields.Prompt: Ainu ceremony in which a bear cub raised in the village is sacrificed and sent back to the gods.
fields.Extra: The bear was a gift from the mountain god Kim-un Kamuy, returned with honour.

fields.Prompt: Ainu word for the spirits and gods that fill the world.
fields.Extra: Kamuy Fuchi is the goddess of the hearth.

fields.Prompt: Ainu oral epics and heroic chants.
fields.Extra: Long sung narratives of gods and heroes, handed down orally — the Ainu had no traditional writing.

fields.Prompt: Female shamans who led religious ritual in the Ryukyu Islands.
fields.Extra: The Ryukyuan creator goddess is Amamikyu.

fields.Prompt: Okinawan guardian figures, half lion and half dog, probably of Chinese inspiration.
fields.Extra: Usually set in pairs on rooftops and gateposts.

fields.Prompt: People who reached northern Kyushu around 1000 BCE, probably from Korea, and brought wet-rice farming and metalworking to Japan.
fields.Extra: Named for the Tokyo neighbourhood where their pottery was first found. Most modern Japanese descend from a mix of Jōmon and Yayoi.

fields.Prompt: Bronze bells of the Yayoi period, often buried on isolated hilltops.
fields.Extra: Perhaps to secure harvests; nobody is sure.

fields.Prompt: Name the Book of Han gives Japan, describing a land of a hundred kingdoms.
fields.Extra: Written with a character meaning something like “dwarf,” which the Japanese later replaced.

fields.Prompt: Gold seal Emperor Guangwu sent to a Japanese ruler in 57 CE, found by a farmer in 1784.
fields.Answer: the King of Na gold seal
fields.Extra: Evidence that the Han recognized a Japanese polity.

fields.Prompt: Qin alchemist said to have sailed east for the elixir of immortality and identified Mount Fuji as the mountain of the immortals.
fields.Extra: Mount Penglai. He sailed for Qin Shi Huang and never came back.

fields.Prompt: Shaman queen who united some thirty Wa polities, described in the Records of Wei.
fields.Extra: She sent tribute to the Wei court and received a hundred bronze mirrors. Her death around 248 closes the Yayoi period.

fields.Prompt: Himiko's domain, whose location is still argued over.
fields.Extra: Kyushu and the Nara basin both have their champions.

fields.Prompt: Probably legendary empress said to have invaded Korea, often linked with Himiko.
fields.Extra: Credited in the chronicles with founding a Japanese base at Mimana.

fields.Prompt: Shinto shrine in Shimane Prefecture dedicated to Ōkuninushi.
fields.Extra: In the Chūgoku region.

fields.Prompt: Holiest shrine of Shinto, dedicated to the sun goddess Amaterasu.
fields.Extra: Ise Jingū, in Mie Prefecture.

fields.Prompt: Legendary first emperor, said to have founded the Japanese state in 660 BCE.
fields.Extra: A descendant of Amaterasu, guided to Yamato by the crow Yatagarasu.

fields.Prompt: Sun goddess from whom the imperial line claims descent.
fields.Extra: Worshipped at Ise. The imperial regalia descend, in the myth, from her gift to her grandson Ninigi.

fields.Prompt: Storm god, brother of Amaterasu.
fields.Extra: With Amaterasu, one of the divine ancestors Emperor Jimmu is said to descend from.

fields.Prompt: Three-legged crow that guided Jimmu to Yamato.
fields.Extra: It is on the crest of the Japan Football Association.

fields.Prompt: Period of about 250–538 CE named for its huge earthen burial mounds.
fields.Extra: Kofun means “old tomb.” The Yamato polity rose in the Nara basin during it.

fields.Prompt: Shape of the grandest kofun, square at the front and round at the back when seen from above.
fields.Extra: Zenpō-kōen-fun.

fields.Prompt: Largest kofun in Japan, in Osaka, attributed to Emperor Nintoku.
fields.Extra: About 460,000 square metres.

fields.Prompt: Nara kofun, perhaps the first keyhole tomb, named for a princess who legendarily stabbed herself with a chopstick.
fields.Extra: “Chopstick tomb.”

fields.Prompt: Terracotta figures of warriors, horses, and houses ranged around kofun.
fields.Extra: Set around the edge of the mound; the name means “clay circle.”

fields.Prompt: Migrants from Korea and China who brought ironworking, silk weaving, and horses to Kofun-era Japan.
fields.Extra: Their skills underpinned the Yamato state, and many court families later claimed descent from them.

fields.Prompt: Imperial regalia sword, called the “grass-cutter.”
fields.Extra: With the mirror Yata no Kagami and the jewel Yasakani no Magatama.

fields.Prompt: Grandson of Amaterasu to whom she gave the three imperial regalia.
fields.Extra: Great-grandfather of Jimmu.

fields.Prompt: Hero thought to fold together the many warriors of the Yamato conquests.
fields.Extra: In the chronicles a son of the legendary Emperor Keikō.

fields.Prompt: Confederacy in southern Korea, between Silla and Baekje, that Yamato used as a foothold.
fields.Extra: Called Mimana in Japanese sources.

fields.Prompt: Goguryeo king's stele whose inscription is evidence of Yamato armies fighting in Korea.
fields.Extra: Yamato sided with Baekje against Goguryeo and Silla.

fields.Prompt: Five Yamato rulers recognized by China in the Book of Song.
fields.Extra: Wa no go-ō.

fields.Prompt: Kingdom whose king sent Yamato a Buddha statue and sutras in 538, introducing Buddhism to Japan.
fields.Extra: The conventional end of the Kofun period and start of the Asuka.

fields.Prompt: Clan that championed Buddhism at the Yamato court.
fields.Extra: Their victory over the Mononobe gave them the court for decades.

fields.Prompt: Clan that opposed Buddhism and lost to the Soga.
fields.Extra: When plague followed the new statue's arrival, it was thrown into a canal.

fields.Prompt: First major Buddhist temple in Japan, built under Soga patronage.
fields.Extra: Also Hōkō-ji. Its Great Buddha of 609 is the oldest dated Buddha image in Japan.

fields.Prompt: Regent credited with the Seventeen-Article Constitution and the Cap and Rank system.
fields.Extra: 574–622. A letter attributed to him calls Japan the land of the rising sun.

fields.Prompt: Temple founded by Prince Shōtoku, with the Tamamushi Shrine, whose buildings are often called the oldest surviving wooden structures in the world.
fields.Extra: Near Nara, with the Hall of Dreams. The Tamamushi Shrine is named for the iridescent beetle wings once set under its metalwork.

fields.Prompt: Temple Prince Shōtoku dedicated to the Four Heavenly Kings.
fields.Extra: In Osaka, by tradition founded in 593.

fields.Prompt: Term for the blending of Buddhism and native Shinto.
fields.Extra: Kami came to be treated as local forms of buddhas; the two were forcibly separated only in 1868.

fields.Prompt: First reigning empress of Japan whose existence is historically secure.
fields.Extra: Prince Shōtoku was her regent.

fields.Prompt: 645 coup in which Prince Naka no Ōe and Nakatomi no Kamatari killed Soga no Iruka.
fields.Extra: It ended Soga power. Kamatari's descendants became the Fujiwara.

fields.Prompt: Reforms after 645 that nationalized land and reorganized government on Chinese lines.
fields.Extra: Named for the era name Taika, “great change” — the first era name Japan used.

fields.Prompt: 672 succession war won by Prince Ōama, who became Emperor Tenmu.
fields.Extra: Decided at the Battle of Seta Bridge against Prince Ōtomo.

fields.Prompt: First Japanese ruler to take the title Tennō.
fields.Extra: Earlier rulers were Ōkimi, “great king.”

fields.Prompt: Code of 701 that formalized a centralized government modelled on Tang China.
fields.Extra: A ritsuryō code of penal and administrative law, headed by a Council of State.

fields.Prompt: Empress who reigned twice, the second time as Saimei.
fields.Extra: The only other ruler to do it is Kōken, who returned as Shōtoku.

fields.Prompt: Planned capital of the late Asuka period, before the move to Nara.
fields.Extra: Japan's first capital on a Chinese-style grid, used 694–710.

fields.Prompt: Capital built at Nara from 710 on the grid plan of Chang'an.
fields.Extra: It gives the Nara period, 710–794, its name.

fields.Prompt: Japan's oldest surviving chronicle, completed in 712.
fields.Extra: “Record of Ancient Matters.” With the Nihon Shoki, the source for the myths and the early emperors.

fields.Prompt: Official history completed in 720, written in classical Chinese.
fields.Extra: Also Nihongi.

fields.Prompt: Oldest anthology of Japanese poetry, compiled in the late eighth century.
fields.Extra: “Collection of Ten Thousand Leaves.”

fields.Prompt: Epidemic of 735–737 that killed perhaps a quarter of Japan's population.
fields.Extra: It killed all four Fujiwara brothers then running the government.

fields.Prompt: Emperor who answered plague and disaster by building Tōdai-ji and its Great Buddha.
fields.Extra: Reigned 724–749. He also ordered a temple and a nunnery in every province.

fields.Prompt: Nara temple housing a sixteen-metre bronze Vairocana, dedicated in 752.
fields.Extra: Its Great Buddha Hall was long the largest wooden building in the world.

fields.Prompt: Popular monk the court first suppressed, then enlisted to raise money, and labour for the Great Buddha.
fields.Extra: Made the first Daisōjō, the highest rank in the Buddhist clergy.

fields.Prompt: Chinese monk who reached Japan on his sixth attempt and set up the ordination platform at Tōdai-ji.
fields.Extra: Jianzhen. He had gone blind on the way.

fields.Prompt: Monk who tried to take the throne in the 760s with the backing of Empress Shōtoku.
fields.Extra: He failed, and the court was wary of monks at court ever after.

fields.Prompt: Korean pottery tradition of about 8000–1500 BCE, named for its comb-scored decoration.
fields.Extra: Jeulmun means “comb-patterned.” It is the Pit-Comb Ware of the peninsula.

fields.Prompt: Early Korean pottery with raised-clay decoration, dating to around 10,000 BCE.
fields.Extra: It precedes the comb-patterned Jeulmun.

fields.Prompt: Korean “plain pottery” period of about 1500–300 BCE, when farming villages and the first chiefdoms appeared.
fields.Extra: Bronze production began in the middle Mumun; iron and elite burials in the late.

fields.Prompt: Megalithic tombs of which the Korean peninsula holds roughly 40 percent of the world's total.
fields.Extra: The Gochang, Hwasun, and Ganghwa dolmen sites are a UNESCO World Heritage site.

fields.Prompt: First Korean kingdom, in the north of the peninsula and southern Manchuria.
fields.Extra: The kingdom, as opposed to the legend, appears in Chinese records from about the 7th century BCE and fell to Emperor Wu of Han in 108 BCE.

fields.Prompt: Legendary founder of Gojoseon, said to have established it in 2333 BCE.
fields.Extra: The date is still counted as the foundation of the Korean nation.

fields.Prompt: Thirteenth-century collection that records the Dangun founding legend.
fields.Extra: Compiled by the monk Iryeon.

fields.Prompt: Son of heaven who told a bear and a tiger to eat mugwort and garlic and avoid the sun for a hundred days.
fields.Extra: Only the bear lasted, and became a woman.

fields.Prompt: The bear who became a woman and bore Dangun to Hwanung.
fields.Extra: The tiger gave up; the bear endured the cave and was rewarded.

fields.Prompt: Bronze vessels said to have been cast by Yu the Great from metal sent by the nine provinces, and handed from dynasty to dynasty as the token of legitimate rule.
fields.Extra: To “ask the weight of the cauldrons” became an idiom for coveting the throne, after King Zhuang of Chu asked it of a Zhou envoy in 606 BCE. They were lost around the Qin conquest.

fields.Prompt: Earliest of the legendary sovereigns, credited with devising the eight trigrams.
fields.Extra: Drawn with a serpent's tail beside his sister and wife, Nüwa: in Han tomb art the pair hold a carpenter's square and a compass, their tails entwined. He is also credited with fishing nets and marriage.

fields.Prompt: Legendary rulers of earliest China, a trio followed by a group of five, whose two titles Qin Shi Huang fused into his new title, huangdi.
fields.Answer: the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors
fields.Extra: Membership varies by source; the Shiji opens with the five, running from the Yellow Emperor to Shun.

fields.Prompt: Legendary sage-king held up by Confucians as the perfect ruler, who passed the throne not to his own son but to a humble man known for filial piety.
fields.Extra: With Shun and Yu he is one of the Three Sage Kings; his abdication, shanrang, became the model of rule by merit.

fields.Prompt: Legendary sage-king famed for his devotion to a father and stepmother who repeatedly tried to kill him.
fields.Extra: Chosen by Yao, he passed the throne in turn to Yu. His father was the blind Gusou, and Shun heads the Twenty-Four Filial Exemplars.

fields.Prompt: Flood-tamer who, in thirteen years of work, passed his own house three times without going in.
fields.Extra: His son Qi inherited the throne, making the Xia the first hereditary dynasty. Yu is honoured with a tomb at Shaoxing, in Zhejiang.

fields.Prompt: Last ruler of the first dynasty, the archetypal wicked last king, overthrown by Tang at Mingtiao.
fields.Extra: Later writers blamed his consort Mo Xi, the first of three “wicked women” whose pattern recurs with Daji of the Shang and Bao Si of the Zhou.

fields.Prompt: Founder of the second Chinese dynasty, who overthrew the last Xia king at Mingtiao.
fields.Extra: Also called Cheng Tang; his chief minister, Yi Yin, was said to have begun as a cook.

fields.Prompt: Shang king who moved the capital to Yin, near modern Anyang, where it stayed until the dynasty fell.
fields.Extra: Hence the Shang's other name, the Yin; the Book of Documents preserves his speeches persuading the people to move.

fields.Prompt: Shang king whose reign opens the oracle-bone record, making him the earliest Chinese ruler attested in writing from his own time.
fields.Extra: Husband of the general Fu Hao. He reigned about 1250–1192 BCE; his name pairs the epithet “martial” with the day-stem ding.

fields.Prompt: Wife of the Shang king Wu Ding who, oracle bones record, led thirteen thousand troops against the Qiang, the largest Shang army on record.
fields.Extra: Her tomb at Anyang, found intact in 1976 and excavated by Zheng Zhenxiang, held 468 bronzes, 755 jades, and nearly 7,000 cowrie shells.

fields.Prompt: Qing scholar who in 1899 recognized ancient writing on “dragon bones” sold as medicine, and so discovered the oracle bones.
fields.Extra: The story goes that he was being treated for malaria. He killed himself in 1900 as the Eight-Nation Alliance entered Beijing.

fields.Prompt: Scholar who in 1917 reconstructed the Shang royal genealogy from oracle bones, showing Sima Qian's list of Shang kings to be largely accurate.
fields.Extra: Also the author of Remarks on Song Lyrics in the Human World; a Qing loyalist, he drowned himself in Kunming Lake at the Summer Palace in 1927.

fields.Prompt: Chinese name for the script on Shang oracle bones, literally “shell and bone writing.”
fields.Extra: Most inscriptions are under fifteen characters. About 4,500 distinct characters are known, and about a third are deciphered.

fields.Prompt: Divination by heating cattle shoulder blades until they cracked, then reading the cracks, practised by the Shang kings.
fields.Extra: With turtle plastrons it is plastromancy. The question, and often the outcome, was carved beside the crack.

fields.Prompt: Count of sixty formed by pairing ten “stems” with twelve “branches,” used by the Shang to name days and later to count years.
fields.Extra: Shang kings took their names from their day-stem, as in Wu Ding; the twelve branches became the zodiac animals.

fields.Prompt: Execution by making victims walk a greased bronze pillar over burning coals, attributed to the last Shang king and his consort Daji.
fields.Extra: Recorded by Sima Qian; Investiture of the Gods makes it a centrepiece of Daji's cruelty.

fields.Prompt: Last king of the dynasty ruling from Anyang, whose ivory chopsticks, according to the Han Feizi, made his uncle Jizi foresee the dynasty's ruin.
fields.Extra: Also called Di Xin; “Zhou” is a pejorative name, unrelated to the Zhou dynasty that overthrew him.

fields.Prompt: Zhou leader imprisoned by the last Shang king at Youli, where tradition says he arranged the sixty-four hexagrams of the Book of Changes.
fields.Extra: Personal name Ji Chang. He died before the conquest, which his son completed, and was named the dynasty's founder after his death.

fields.Prompt: Son of the Zhou leader imprisoned at Youli, who destroyed the Shang at Muye around 1046 BCE and became the first Zhou king.
fields.Extra: Personal name Ji Fa. He died soon after, leaving his brother the Duke of Zhou as regent for his young son.

fields.Prompt: Chronicle written on slips, found around 280 CE in the tomb of a Wei king at Ji, giving a chronology from the Xia to the Warring States independent of Sima Qian.
fields.Extra: Also called the Jizhong Annals; the surviving “current text” is suspected of later reworking.

fields.Prompt: State-funded Chinese research effort of 1996–2000 that dated the first dynasty to 2070 BCE and the Battle of Muye to 1046 BCE.
fields.Extra: Its dates are widely used in China but disputed by many Western scholars.

fields.Prompt: Oldest classic of Chinese medicine, a dialogue between the Yellow Emperor and his physician Qi Bo, compiled around the Han.
fields.Extra: In English, The Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic; it sets out yin and yang and the Five Phases in the body.

fields.Prompt: Earliest surviving Chinese pharmacopoeia, listing 365 drugs, attributed to the divine farmer but compiled in the Han.
fields.Extra: Its drugs are ranked in three grades, from nourishing to poisonous.

fields.Prompt: System of wood, fire, earth, metal, and water, matched with colours, directions, and dynasties; earth, at the centre, gave emperors their yellow.
fields.Extra: In Chinese, wuxing; systematized by Zou Yan in the Warring States. The Qin claimed water and wore black.

fields.Prompt: Archaeologist who led the Academia Sinica's excavations at Anyang from 1928, the first scientific digs in China.
fields.Extra: Often called the father of Chinese archaeology; he took the collections to Taiwan in 1949.

fields.Prompt: Title of Chinese rulers from the Zhou onward, meaning “Son of Heaven,” for the one who governs tianxia, “all under heaven.”
fields.Extra: It ties the ruler's authority to the Mandate of Heaven.

fields.Prompt: Mythic war god with a bronze forehead and many arms who led the Jiuli against the Yellow Emperor at Zhuolu.
fields.Extra: He raised a magic fog, and the Yellow Emperor's south-pointing chariot found the way through it.

fields.Prompt: Giant whose body became the mountains, rivers, sun, and moon after he spent 18,000 years pushing sky and earth apart.
fields.Extra: His breath became the wind and his voice the thunder; the story is first written down in the third century CE.

fields.Prompt: Legendary “Flame Emperor” who tasted hundreds of plants in a day to learn which were food, medicine, or poison.
fields.Extra: Often identified with Yan Di; the Chinese call themselves descendants of Yan and Huang, him and the Yellow Emperor.

fields.Prompt: Legendary ruler whose name was borrowed for the oldest classic of Chinese medicine, and from whom the Chinese call themselves descended.
fields.Extra: His colour is the yellow of earth, the central phase, which later emperors wore as theirs; a tomb honours him in Shaanxi.

fields.Prompt: Shang divination records dug up around Anyang and ground into traditional medicine as longgu, “dragon” remedies, until a scholar noticed the writing in 1899.
fields.Extra: Wang Yirong made the identification; the Academia Sinica began scientific excavation in 1928.

fields.Prompt: Strategist to Kings Wen and Wu, enfeoffed with the state of Qi after the conquest, and credited with the military text Six Secret Teachings.
fields.Extra: Also called Taigong Wang or Lü Shang; in Investiture of the Gods he presides over the deification of the war dead.

fields.Prompt: Brother of King Wu, credited with the Rites of Zhou and with building the eastern capital that became Luoyang.
fields.Extra: His son was enfeoffed with Lu, the state Confucius was born in. The Rites of Zhou itself is now thought to be centuries later.

fields.Prompt: Clash of 1046 BCE at which the Shang army, much of it pressed captives, is said to have turned its weapons on its own side.
fields.Extra: The last Shang king then burned himself in his palace at Yin.

fields.Prompt: Ming novel of the war between the last Shang king and the rising Zhou, in which Daji is a possessing fox spirit and the fallen become deities.
fields.Extra: In Chinese, Fengshen Yanyi; the source of Nezha's modern fame.

fields.Prompt: Compendium commissioned around 239 BCE by the Qin chancellor Lü Buwei, who offered a thousand pieces of gold to anyone who could improve it by a single character.
fields.Extra: In English, Master Lü's Spring and Autumn Annals; it lists Mo Xi among the wicked women of antiquity.

fields.Prompt: Consort of the last Xia king, the first of the “wicked women” later writers blamed for a dynasty's fall.
fields.Extra: The pattern repeats with Daji of the Shang and Bao Si of the Zhou.

fields.Prompt: Chu minister and poet who drowned himself in the Miluo River after the Qin sacked his state's capital, a death the Dragon Boat Festival commemorates.
fields.Extra: Traditionally the author of the Li Sao, the longest poem in the Chu Ci.

fields.Prompt: Long poem in which a slandered official, dressed in fragrant plants, journeys through the heavens in search of a worthy match.
fields.Extra: “Encountering Sorrow”; traditionally by Qu Yuan, and the centrepiece of the Chu Ci.

fields.Prompt: Anthology of shamanistic southern verse, compiled in the Han, that stands beside the Classic of Poetry as the second fountainhead of Chinese poetry.
fields.Extra: The Songs of the South, or Songs of Chu.

fields.Prompt: Han scholar who persuaded Emperor Wu to make Confucianism the state orthodoxy, fusing it with yin–yang and Five Phases cosmology.
fields.Extra: His Luxuriant Dew of the Spring and Autumn Annals reads Heaven's will in portents and disasters.

fields.Prompt: Han palace lady married to the Xiongnu chanyu Huhanye under the heqin policy, one of the Four Beauties.
fields.Extra: Legend says a court painter made her portrait plain because she would not bribe him, so the emperor saw her beauty only as she left; hers is the face that made geese fall from the sky.

fields.Prompt: Han tombs at Changsha whose finds include the preserved body of the Marquise of Dai and silk manuscripts of the Daodejing.
fields.Extra: Excavated 1972–1974; the T-shaped silk banner from Lady Dai's tomb maps heaven, earth, and the underworld.

fields.Prompt: Historian who wrote the Book of Han, the first history devoted to a single dynasty, and died in prison before finishing it.
fields.Extra: His sister Ban Zhao completed it; his twin brother was the general Ban Chao.

fields.Prompt: Luoyang temple held to be the first Buddhist temple in China, founded after Emperor Ming of Han dreamed of a golden figure.
fields.Extra: Named for the white horse said to have carried the first sutras from the west, around 68 CE.

fields.Prompt: Eastern Han physician said to have operated under a herbal anaesthetic and to have been executed by Cao Cao.
fields.Extra: The anaesthetic is mafeisan. In the novel he scrapes poison from Guan Yu's arm bone while Guan Yu plays Go.

fields.Prompt: Oath of brotherhood sworn by Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei in the opening chapter of Romance of the Three Kingdoms.
fields.Answer: the Oath of the Peach Garden
fields.Extra: Fiction: the histories record the three as close, not as sworn brothers.

fields.Prompt: Wei scholars, among them Ji Kang and Ruan Ji, who withdrew from office into wine, music, and Daoist “pure conversation.”
fields.Answer: the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove
fields.Extra: Ji Kang was executed in 262; he is said to have played the zither piece Guangling san before he died.
fields.Entity: Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove

fields.Prompt: Jin calligrapher, the “Sage of Calligraphy,” whose preface to the poems of a gathering at the Orchid Pavilion in 353 is the most famous work of Chinese calligraphy.
fields.Extra: Emperor Taizong of Tang loved the original Lanting Xu so much that he was buried with it; only copies survive.

fields.Prompt: Eastern Jin painter known through copies of the handscroll Admonitions of the Instructress to the Court Ladies.
fields.Extra: The best-known copy is in the British Museum; Nymph of the Luo River is also attributed to him.

fields.Prompt: Jin poet who quit office rather than bow to a superior for a salary, and wrote of a fisherman who finds a hidden utopia beyond a grove of peach trees.
fields.Extra: Also Tao Qian. The story is “Peach Blossom Spring”; he is the great poet of farming, wine, and chrysanthemums.

fields.Prompt: Chinese monk who walked to India in 399 in search of the monastic rules and came home by sea through Sri Lanka.
fields.Extra: His Record of Buddhist Kingdoms is a key source on Gupta India.

fields.Prompt: Kuchean monk brought to Chang'an in 401 whose translations of the Lotus and Diamond Sutras became the standard Chinese Buddhist scriptures.
fields.Extra: Held for years by the general who captured him, he was forced to marry; his translation bureau worked under the Later Qin.

fields.Prompt: Indian monk traditionally credited with bringing Chan Buddhism to China, and with nine years of meditation facing a cave wall near the Shaolin Temple.
fields.Extra: Daruma in Japan, where the round red Daruma dolls represent him.

fields.Prompt: Buddhist cave temples near Dunhuang, begun in 366, whose sealed Library Cave yielded tens of thousands of manuscripts in 1900.
fields.Extra: Aurel Stein and Paul Pelliot carried off much of the library, including the printed Diamond Sutra of 868.

fields.Prompt: Buddhist scripture whose copy dated 868, found at Dunhuang, is the oldest dated printed book in the world.
fields.Extra: A woodblock-printed scroll, now in the British Library.

fields.Prompt: Illiterate woodcutter who became the Sixth Patriarch of Chan by answering a rival's verse, which likened the mind to a mirror to be wiped clean of dust, with one saying that since nothing exists, there is nowhere for dust to fall.
fields.Extra: His teaching of sudden enlightenment is recorded in the Platform Sutra.

fields.Prompt: Tang essayist exiled for his “Memorial on the Bone of the Buddha,” which opposed the court's veneration of a relic.
fields.Extra: A champion of plain “ancient-style” prose and a forerunner of Neo-Confucianism.

fields.Prompt: Tang poet of Song of Everlasting Sorrow and Song of the Pipa, who is said to have wanted his verse understood by an old peasant woman.
fields.Extra: Po Chü-i in Wade-Giles; enormously popular in Heian Japan.

fields.Prompt: Failed examination candidate and salt smuggler whose rebellion took Chang'an in 881 and left the Tang a shell.
fields.Extra: His army is said to have massacred the foreign merchants of Guangzhou in 879; Zhu Wen began as one of his officers.

fields.Prompt: Campaign of 845 under Emperor Wuzong that closed thousands of monasteries and returned hundreds of thousands of monks and nuns to lay life.
fields.Extra: Also the Huichang persecution, after the era name; Buddhism in China never regained its Tang wealth.

fields.Prompt: Lead-glazed Tang pottery in amber, green, and cream, made mostly for tombs: camels, horses, and foreign grooms.
fields.Extra: “Three colours”; the camels with Central Asian riders are the classic image of the Silk Road.

fields.Prompt: Founder of Daoism, said to have been an archivist at the Zhou court who wrote down his teaching for a border guard as he left for the west.
fields.Extra: “Old Master.” The Shiji says Confucius visited him and afterwards compared him to a dragon.

fields.Prompt: General said to have served King Helü of Wu, and credited with a treatise holding that all warfare is based on deception.
fields.Extra: Sunzi. To prove discipline, the story goes, he beheaded two of the king's concubines who laughed at drill.

fields.Prompt: Thinker who taught impartial care for all, jian'ai, and led a band of engineers who helped cities defend themselves against aggressors.
fields.Extra: Mo Di; his school, Mohism, rivalled Confucianism until the Qin.

fields.Prompt: King who slept on brushwood and tasted gall to keep his humiliation fresh, then after twenty years destroyed the state of Wu.
fields.Extra: His sword, still sharp and barely tarnished, was excavated in Hubei in 1965.

fields.Prompt: Consort whom King You of Zhou amused by lighting the war beacons, so that no one came when the Quanrong really attacked.
fields.Extra: The third of the “wicked women,” after Mo Xi and Daji; the beacon story is probably a later invention.

fields.Prompt: Oldest collection of Chinese poetry, 305 poems of the Zhou in three sections of Airs, Odes, and Hymns, said to have been selected by Confucius.
fields.Extra: The Shijing, or Book of Songs; one of the Five Classics.

fields.Prompt: Standard script that Li Si imposed across the empire in place of the regional scripts of the Warring States.
fields.Extra: Xiaozhuan. Clerical script, already used by Qin scribes, soon replaced it for everyday writing.

fields.Prompt: God who, washing himself clean after fleeing the land of the dead, produced Amaterasu from his left eye, Tsukuyomi from his right, and Susanoo from his nose.
fields.Extra: With his sister and wife, Izanami, he stirred the sea with a jewelled spear to make the first island, Onogoro.

fields.Prompt: Goddess who died giving birth to the fire god, and chased her husband out of Yomi, the land of the dead, when he broke his promise not to look at her rotting body.
fields.Extra: She vowed to kill a thousand people a day; he answered that he would cause fifteen hundred to be born.

fields.Prompt: Moral code of 604 attributed to Prince Shōtoku, opening with the injunction that harmony is to be valued.
fields.Extra: Not a constitution in the modern sense: Confucian and Buddhist precepts for officials.

fields.Prompt: Courtier who plotted the 645 coup against the Soga with Prince Naka no Ōe, and was granted the surname Fujiwara on his deathbed.
fields.Extra: Founder of the Fujiwara, who dominated the court for centuries.

fields.Prompt: Prince Naka no Ōe as emperor: leader of the Taika Reforms, who moved the capital to Ōmi.
fields.Extra: His death in 671 set off the Jinshin War between his son and his brother.

fields.Prompt: Japanese embassies to the Tang court, which brought back Buddhist texts, law codes, and city plans.
fields.Extra: Some fifteen voyages between 630 and 838; Kūkai and Saichō sailed with the 804 mission.

fields.Prompt: Japanese student who passed the Tang examinations, served Xuanzong for decades, and was mourned in a poem by Li Bai after a false report that he had drowned.
fields.Extra: Shipwrecked off Annam, he survived and died in Chang'an without seeing Japan again; his poem on the moon over Mount Mikasa is in the Hyakunin Isshu.

fields.Prompt: Log treasure house at Tōdai-ji holding the possessions Empress Kōmyō dedicated after Emperor Shōmu's death, many brought along the Silk Road.
fields.Extra: Built of interlocking triangular logs; its treasures, from a Persian glass bowl to a five-stringed lute, are shown once a year in Nara.

fields.Prompt: Emperor who moved the capital out of Nara, first to Nagaoka and in 794 to Heian-kyō, partly to escape the Nara monasteries.
fields.Extra: The move ends the Nara period and opens the Heian.

fields.Prompt: Greatest poet of the Man'yōshū, whose long poems for the court of Empress Jitō later made him revered as a god of poetry.
fields.Extra: Master of the chōka, the long poem.

fields.Prompt: Poet and courtier generally credited with compiling the Man'yōshū, whose own poems make up the largest share of it.
fields.Extra: Over 470 of its poems are his.

fields.Prompt: Refugee from the state of Yan who seized the throne of Gojoseon around 194 BCE, founding the dynasty the Han destroyed in 108 BCE.
fields.Extra: His grandson Ugeo was the last king; the Han set up four commanderies in its place.

fields.Prompt: Longest-lived of the four commanderies the Han set up in northern Korea in 108 BCE, centred near Pyongyang.
fields.Extra: Nangnang in Korean; Goguryeo took it in 313.

fields.Prompt: Shang prince said to have fled to Korea when his dynasty fell and founded a state there, a story modern Korean historians reject.
fields.Extra: Jizi, the uncle who foresaw King Zhou's ruin; Joseon-era Confucians took Gija Joseon seriously.

fields.Prompt: Late Tang poet of dense, allusive love poems, many of them titled simply “Untitled.”
fields.Extra: His “Brocade Zither” is famously obscure. He and Du Mu are the “Little Li and Du,” after Li Bai and Du Fu.

fields.Prompt: Tang poet of “Spring Dawn,” whose speaker sleeps through daybreak, hears birds everywhere, and wonders how many blossoms fell in the night's wind and rain.
fields.Extra: An older friend of Li Bai and Wang Wei, and with Wang Wei the model of Tang landscape poetry.

fields.Prompt: Hermit poet named for the Tiantai peak he lived on, whose verses Gary Snyder translated in 1958.
fields.Extra: “Cold Mountain.” Jack Kerouac dedicated The Dharma Bums to him.

fields.Prompt: Anthology compiled around 1763 by Sun Zhu, long the standard primer of classical Chinese verse.
fields.Extra: Tangshi sanbai shou. Du Fu is its best-represented poet.
